**7.7 Magnitude Earthquake Rocks Northern Chile, Killing at Least 12**

*Coastal communities assess damage as tsunami warnings lifted after hours of uncertainty*

SANTIAGO, Chile — A powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of northern Chile early Thursday, killing at least 12 people, injuring dozens more, and sending residents fleeing into the streets as buildings swayed and cracked across the region.

The quake struck at approximately 3:47 a.m. local time, with its epicenter located roughly 55 miles northwest of the port city of Iquique, according to Chile's National Seismological Center. The tremor was felt as far south as Santiago, more than 1,000 miles away, and prompted evacuation orders along much of the country's northern coastline.

Chile's Interior Ministry confirmed the death toll Thursday afternoon, with officials cautioning that the number could rise as search and rescue teams continue combing through collapsed structures in the hardest-hit areas. At least 85 people have been treated for injuries ranging from minor cuts to severe trauma caused by falling debris.

The National Emergency Office initially issued a tsunami warning for the entire Chilean coastline, triggering mass evacuations in low-lying areas. The warning was lifted roughly three hours later after only minor sea level fluctuations were recorded, but not before tens of thousands of residents spent hours sheltering in higher ground.

"This was a night none of us will forget," said Iquique Mayor Mirta Ampuero during a press conference outside the city's emergency operations center. "We have lost neighbors, we have lost homes, and we have lost a sense of safety that will take time to rebuild. But I have seen this community come together in the darkest hours, and that gives me hope."

In the nearby town of Alto Hospicio, which sustained some of the most severe structural damage, Mayor Patricio Ferreira described scenes of devastation.

"Entire blocks of housing have crumbled. We have families who lost everything in a matter of seconds," Ferreira said. "Our first priority right now is making sure everyone is accounted for. After that, we begin the long process of rebuilding."

Chilean President Gabriel Boric addressed the nation Thursday morning, declaring a state of emergency in the Tarapacá and Antofagasta regions and mobilizing military resources to assist with relief efforts.

"Chile has faced earthquakes before, and we know how to respond with resilience and solidarity," Boric said. "We will not leave any affected family without support."

Chile sits along the Pacific Ring of Fire, one of the most seismically active regions on Earth, and has a long history of devastating earthquakes, including a 8.8 magnitude quake in 2010 that killed hundreds and caused billions of dollars in damage. Building codes implemented after that disaster are credited with limiting the scale of destruction in Thursday's quake, though officials say the toll would likely have been far higher in a country with less stringent construction standards.

Aftershocks continued to rattle the region throughout the day, with seismologists warning residents to remain vigilant. The strongest aftershock, measuring 5.9, struck roughly six hours after the initial quake.

International aid organizations, including the Red Cross and USAID, have pledged support, with search-and-rescue teams and medical supplies expected to arrive in the region within 48 hours.

Officials are asking residents to avoid unnecessary travel into affected zones as emergency crews work to restore power, clear debris, and assess the structural integrity of damaged buildings. Shelters have been set up in Iquique, Alto Hospicio, and Antofagasta for displaced families.

This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

President Gabriel Boric addressed the nation in a televised statement, urging calm while pledging full government support for affected regions.

"This is a difficult moment for our country, but Chile has faced these challenges before, and we will rebuild," Boric said. "We are mobilizing all available resources — military, medical, and logistical — to assist those affected. No community will be left behind."

The president also thanked international partners for offers of assistance, noting that Chile has activated its national disaster response protocols, which were significantly strengthened after previous devastating earthquakes.

## Aid Workers on the Ground

International aid organizations, including the Red Cross, have deployed teams to assist with emergency shelter, medical care, and food distribution.

"The immediate need right now is shelter and clean water," said Elena Ramirez, a coordinator with the Chilean Red Cross. "Many families have lost their homes entirely, and with aftershocks continuing, people are afraid to return to damaged buildings even if they're still standing."

Ramirez added that mental health support would also be a critical part of the response in the coming weeks. "Earthquakes leave scars that aren't just physical," she said. "Communities need psychological support as much as they need food and shelter."

## A Familiar, Painful History

Chile sits along the Pacific "Ring of Fire," one of the most seismically active regions in the world, and this week's quake is a stark reminder of the country's turbulent history with earthquakes.

The 1960 Valdivia earthquake remains the most powerful ever recorded, measuring 9.5 in magnitude and killing an estimated 1,600 people while triggering tsunamis that reached as far as Japan and Hawaii. More recently, the 2010 Maule earthquake, an 8.8-magnitude quake, killed more than 500 people and caused widespread destruction across central Chile, exposing gaps in the country's building codes and emergency response systems.

In the years since, Chile has invested heavily in earthquake preparedness, including stricter building codes, early-warning systems, and public education campaigns — measures that experts say likely reduced casualties in this latest disaster.

"Chile is, unfortunately, one of the most experienced countries in the world when it comes to earthquakes," said seismologist Dr. Fernando Vidal. "The infrastructure improvements made after 2010 have undoubtedly saved lives this time. But no amount of preparation can fully protect against a quake of this magnitude."

## Looking Ahead

As of Tuesday evening, tsunami warnings had been downgraded for most coastal areas, though officials continue to urge caution as aftershocks are expected in the coming days. Rescue teams remain focused on reaching remote communities, while shelters have been set up in schools and community centers for displaced residents.

For many Chileans, the earthquake is a grim echo of past tragedies — but also a test of the resilience the country has built in the decades since.

"We've been through this before," said Gonzalez, the La Serena shop owner, standing outside her damaged store. "We will rebuild again. That's what we do."
